In Indonesia, when a friend flies to Tokyo, the whole group chat asks them to bring something back. It's called jastip. And someone always ends up fronting the money.
Either friends pay upfront for things that might be sold out, or the traveller pays for everything, and chases friends for weeks.
Jastip fixes the money with PayPal. Friends approve a hold, up to a max price. One receipt sets each friend's exact charge. Anything not found is released.
Dina is flying to Tokyo next week. She opens a trip, sets her fee per item, and shares one link with her friends' group chat.
Ayu pastes a TikTok link. AI turns it into the product, the variant, and a typical Tokyo shelf price, so she can set her max with confidence. She also picks what happens if it's sold out.

Dina accepts the asks, and picks her shopping day. Now Ayu approves a PayPal hold, for her max plus Dina's fee. This is the real PayPal sandbox, with Ayu's Indonesian account, paying in yen. Nothing is charged yet. It's an authorization, made with PayPal's Orders API.
In the shop, Dina ticks items off as she finds them. The patches aren't on the shelf. The eight pack of Tokyo Banana is sold out, so she offers the four pack, and Bima accepts it from his phone.
At the till, Dina photographs one receipt. AI reads every Japanese line, and matches each line to a friend. Code, not AI, works out the money: the line plus the fee, never above the hold.

One tap. PayPal captures each friend's exact amount from their hold, and voids the hold for the patches Dina couldn't find. Ayu paid exactly her line plus the fee. The rest of her hold was never taken.
Back home, Ayu taps, I got my item. That's the delivery record for both of them.
No one pays upfront. No one is overcharged. Every money rule is enforced in code, and it all runs on the PayPal sandbox today. Jastip. Shop abroad for friends.
